div: The detector efficiency (a detector response function, or DRF) tells InterSpec what fraction of the gammas from a source are recorded in each full-energy peak. Activity, shielding and detection-limit calculations need one. When a spectrum is opened, InterSpec picks one automatically if it can: the one you chose before for that detector's serial number or model, else a built-in detector of the same type.

Open this dialog with Tools → Detector Response Select, or by clicking the detector name (
) shown in tools such as Activity/Shielding Fit, Gamma XS Calc and Reference Photopeaks. Changing the detector in any of these places is the same.

The Library The Library lists every detector InterSpec knows about: the ones that ship with it, ones found in the standard folders of GADRAS, ISOCS and ANGLE (on Windows) and in InterSpec's own folder, and the ones you have made or used. Detectors are grouped as Suggested for this spectrum (chosen before for this serial number or model, included in the spectrum file, or InterSpec's default for this type of detector), Recently used, and Everything else. Search by name, crystal, model or file; the chips below the search show only detectors from one source, or only those with a recorded crystal geometry.
Customized copies of a detector (see below) are listed under the detector they were made from; click Show N customized copies to see them.
The list is re-checked each time the dialog opens: files that changed are read again, and the rest come from memory, so the dialog opens quickly.

Previewing and using a detector Clicking a detector only previews it: its efficiency curve is drawn as a solid line, with the detector in use drawn dashed for comparison, and What it includes lists what it can do. Nothing changes until you click Use “…”; closing the dialog (or Cancel) never applies a detector you only previewed. A change can be undone with Edit → Undo.
Rel. eff. is the full-energy-peak efficiency at 1332 keV for a Co-60 point source 25 cm away, as a percent of a 3×3 inch NaI(Tl) detector (the IEEE 325 definition).
far-field only detectors scale their efficiency by the solid angle, which is fine for sources more than a few detector diameters away on the detector axis. near-field OK detectors have a modeled response, so close and off-axis sources are handled too. fixed geometry detectors are only valid for the setup they were made for.
Tick Also pick it automatically next time to have this detector chosen for spectra from the same serial number or detector model.
Customize a copy… makes your own copy of a detector, to rename it, give it a crystal geometry and Monte-Carlo response, fit its peak widths to your spectra, or anchor it to a measured efficiency. The copy is saved under Made by you.
XML downloads the detector (including any Monte-Carlo response); QR code shows it as a code another InterSpec can scan. Detectors you made can be deleted.

Import The Import tab brings in a detector from a file, or from a formula; or use Or make one from calibration spectra to fit one to peaks from known sources (the Make Detector Response tool). An imported detector is previewed before you use it, and once used it is saved under Made by you.

li.div:
The "Rel. Eff." detector response functions are specified using CSV or TSV files that provide detector dimensions and relative efficiencies at a given distance. A single CSV or TSV file may contain multiple lines with each line specifying a DRF. The format of the file is:
Lines starting with the string "#credit:" will be displayed to the user to provide context/credit/information about the DRFs contained in the file. XHTML may be used in the descriptions. Lines otherwise starting with a "#" character will be ignored.
The relative efficiency is specified using an equation of the form:
exp( c0 + c1*x1 + c2*x2 + c3*x3 + c4*x4 + c5*x5 + c6*x6 + c7*x7)
Where x is the energy in MeV, and c0, c1, etc are specified in the CSV or TSV file.
Tables in InterSpec's own folders are listed in the Library automatically; others can be imported.
The columns in the CSV/TSV are:
1: Display Name 2: Eff rel. to 3x3 NaI 3: Name 4: c0 5: c1 6: c2 7: c3 8: c4 9: c5 10: c6 11: c7 12: p0 (unused) 13: p1 (unused) 14: p2 (unused) 15: Calib Distance (cm) 16: Radius (cm)

Drop a detector efficiency file onto the area on this tab, or click it to browse for the file. While this tab is showing, files dropped elsewhere in InterSpec are ignored, rather than being opened as spectra. The type of file is recognized automatically, and the options that apply to it are shown. Accepted files are:
InterSpec detector responses, as XML or CSV (for example, as exported from this dialog, or from the Make Detector Response tool).
A "GADRAS" Efficiency.csv, optionally with its Detector.dat. The Detector.dat adds the detector diameter, peak width response, peak shape, and crystal geometry; with the geometry, efficiencies are also available for sources off to the side of, or close to, the detector.
A "GADRAS" Detector.dat by itself. This describes the detector, but not its efficiency, so either add its Efficiency.csv, or click Compute efficiency… to compute it with a Monte-Carlo simulation.
A .par full-energy-peak efficiency grid, together with its DETECTOR.txt geometry file; both are required. If the DETECTOR.txt describes several detectors, the one naming the .par file is used, or you will be asked to choose. The grid has no total efficiency, which cascade-summing corrections need; add one by Monte Carlo with Customize a copy…, on its "Geom & MC" tab.
An ISOCS .ecc file, or an ANGLE file. If an ANGLE file describes the detector as well as a measured reference efficiency, it can be used as a "generic detector", so efficiencies are available for any source position.
A relative-efficiency or GammaQuant list of detectors; choose the one to use.
A CSV file of energies and efficiencies. The first column is the energy in keV, and the second is the efficiency; a header line saying whether the efficiency is a percentage or a fraction is recommended, for example:
Energy (keV), Efficiency (%)
10, 0.0
20,10.3
25,28.3
...
For a detector described by two files, drop (or select) both at once, or drop the second file on the area that asks for it. When this dialog is not open, both files can also be dropped onto InterSpec together.
For a file that lists efficiencies, choose how they are to be interpreted: as intrinsic efficiencies (for gammas striking the detector face, which needs the detector diameter), as absolute efficiencies at a given distance, or for a fixed source geometry. The detector name defaults to the file name, and can be edited. After using it, Customize a copy… lets you further edit the imported detector.

When evaluating efficiencies for energies between the provided values, Akima Interpolation is used. This interpolation method was chosen as it is continually differentiable, only uses data from next neighbor points to determine value, and does not suffer from the same overshoots or oscillations that polynomial splines (e.g. third order splines) suffer from.
A comparison of Akima, Cubic Spline, and linear interpolation methods for a set of intrinsic efficiency pairs provided by "GADRAS" for a hand-held detector.
Note: we have to improve this chart!

If either the intrinsic or absolute efficiency is known as a mathematical function of energy (represented by "×" in the input function), it may be entered here; the detector diameter must also be known. The formula entered may use energy in either keV or MeV as long as the appropriate check box is selected. The evaluated formula should yield a number between 0 and 1 for the energy range it is valid in. The input formula must be a function of a single variable (energy) represented as a "×" in the formula.
Intrinsic efficiency formulas represent the fraction of gammas which strike the detector face, that will end up in the full energy photopeak of the gammas incident energy.
Absolute efficiency formulas represent the fraction of gammas that leave the source, which will be recorded in their full energy photopeak, at a specified distance; hence when this efficiency is selected you will also have to enter a distance the input formula corresponds to.
Valid Equations: Equations that can be entered follow standard mathematical rules, and can make use of the following functions:
abs, sqrt, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, ln (synonym for log) , log10
and functions that take two arguments : min, max, pow
The following arithmetic operators may be used: +, - , /, *, ^, **
The following logical operators may be used: ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, &&, ||
Logical operations result in a value of 0.0 if false, and 1.0 if true, and may be chained together, ex.
0.5*(x<50||x>100) + 0.75*(x>=50&&x<=100) will result in a function with value of 0.75 between 50 and 100, and 0.5 everywhere else.
An example input formula could be:
exp(-343.63 + 269.10*log(x) -83.80*ln(x)^2 + 13.00*pow(log(x),3) -1.01*log(x)^4)
As a shortcut, for efficiencies of the form
exp(C0 + C1*log(x) + C2*log(x)^2 + ... ) you can enter just the coefficients, and when you click the Set button, the equation will be tranformed for you. This is useful when copy-pasting the coefficients from a spreadsheet. The numbers can be seperated by commas, spaces, tabs, newlines, or semi-colons. For example, if you enter
-9.811E+00 -7.99E-01 4.618E-02 2.81E-03 -1.9432E-02 0.000E+00 0.000E+00
Then once you click the Set button, the text will be transformed into:
exp( -9.811E+00 + -7.99E-01*log(x) + 4.618E-02*log(x)^2 + 2.81E-03*log(x)^3 + -1.9432E-02*log(x)^4 )
As you type, the formula is checked, its efficiency at 662 keV shown, and its curve drawn in the preview, so you can see it is reasonable before using it. Instead of a formula, you can choose Coefficients of the standard form and enter (or paste from a spreadsheet) just the coefficients. An efficiency that is absolute at a given distance, or for a fixed geometry, and the energy range the formula is valid for, are under More options….

Detectors you import, enter as a formula, make from calibration spectra, or customize are saved inside InterSpec and listed under Made by you. It is a good idea to give them names you will recognize later.
